nameStory: The shiny cinnamon polypore gets its name from its gorgeous rusty-brown color that looks just like ground cinnamon spice, combined with its glossy, almost varnished appearance when fresh. The word 'polypore' refers to its underside, which is covered in tiny pores instead of gills - like a natural sponge with microscopic holes.
description: This is a small to medium-sized bracket fungus that grows like a shelf or funnel from dead wood. The shiny cinnamon polypore typically measures 2-6 inches across with a distinctive glossy, cinnamon-brown surface that catches the light beautifully. Unlike many bracket fungi that are tough and woody, this species has a somewhat leathery texture. It's an annual fungus, meaning each fruiting body lasts just one growing season before decomposing.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Bright cinnamon to rusty-brown color with a distinctive shiny, almost lacquered appearance when fresh. Surface has concentric zones of color and feels smooth to the touch with a leathery texture.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny circular pores (not gills) that are cream to pale brown, bruising darker when pressed. The pore surface feels slightly soft and spongy.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Often has a short, stubby stem that's the same cinnamon color as the cap, though sometimes grows directly from wood without a visible stem.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, mild mushroomy smell with no unpleasant odors. Older specimens may smell slightly musty.

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Pore surface darkens to brown or blackish when bruised or scratched, though this reaction may be slow to develop.

habitat: Found growing on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and fallen branches in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. Particularly common on oak, maple, and birch wood in moist woodland areas. Prefers partially shaded locations where the wood stays consistently damp but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: New fruiting bodies begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm and moisture increases. Fresh specimens show their brightest, most glossy cinnamon coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when most specimens are found. Look for the characteristic shiny surface that's most pronounced during humid summer weather.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting into early fall, though specimens may start losing their glossy shine and become more weathered-looking as they age.
seasonality.winter: Old fruiting bodies may persist on logs but become dried, brittle, and lose their distinctive shiny appearance. Not actively growing.

funFact: Despite being called 'shiny,' this fungus actually gets duller and more matte as it ages, meaning the most beautiful specimens are often the youngest ones - it's like finding nature's fresh coat of varnish before it weathers away!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the brown funnel polypore (Coltricia perennis), but the shiny cinnamon polypore has a much more glossy, lacquered appearance when fresh. Memory trick: 'Shiny cinnamon' literally describes what you're looking for - if it's not noticeably glossy and cinnamon-colored, it's probably something else.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Coltricia' honors Italian botanist Coltricio, while 'cinnamomea' directly refers to its cinnamon color. This genus was once grouped with other polypores but is now recognized as having unique characteristics that set it apart from typical bracket fungi.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative, the brown funnel polypore (Coltricia perennis), the shiny cinnamon polypore is much glossier when fresh and tends to be more shelf-like rather than funnel-shaped. The brown funnel polypore also tends to be more consistently funnel-shaped and lacks the distinctive lacquered shine. Both species fruit on dead wood, but the shiny cinnamon polypore's surface literally looks like it's been polished.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Brown Funnel Polypore differs from its cousin the Shiny Cinnamon Polypore by its deeper funnel shape and less glossy surface texture.
